description: We’re a group of students building a web tool that lets anyone chase their curiosity about space, because we believe everyone should have an equal shot at making the next big discovery.
summary: Tombaugh is a free web tool that lets anyone hunt for moving objects in NASA's SPHEREx sky photos, the way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by blinking two photographs. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we align SPHEREx frames to Gaia stars and judge each pixel against its own measured noise, which cuts false residuals from 183 to 0 per frame in our worst test field, and recovers a real asteroid, 120 Lachesis, matching JPL. It matters because the SPHEREx archive is too large for a few experts to inspect by eye, so giving the public careful tools and a candidate-checking process widens who can take part, while keeping unverified claims away from the people who study them.
details:
Tombaugh is a free web tool built by students (team Grand Larpers) who love looking up. Press "What's moving above you?" and it finds the patch of sky straight above you and shows it as SPHEREx recorded it on earlier dates (not a live view). Your exact location never leaves your device. The default "Plate" view is a negative, like the photographic plates astronomers used in Tombaugh's day, and one click switches to a "Sky" view.

How it works: frames are aligned to Gaia stars, resampled to a common grid and stacked per visit. We first expected a per-pixel wavelength fit to remove the false residuals that make a blind search unusable. We tested that and it did not help on its own. What does help is judging each pixel against its own measured scatter, because SPHEREx pixels are larger than a star image and each frame samples a star differently. Residual peaks per frame fall from 183 to 0 (Barnard D3), 53 to 0.6 (Epsilon Indi B D2) and 12 to 2.3 (WISE 0855 D5).

Validation: measured motions are close to published values (WISE 0855 7.51 +/- 0.57 vs 8.15 arcsec/yr, Barnard's Star 11.04 +/- 0.82 vs 10.39, Epsilon Indi B 4.57 +/- 0.08 vs 4.70). Our Singapore demo field contains asteroid 120 Lachesis, recovered at 27.34 +/- 0.05 arcsec/hr vs JPL's 27.37, and a blind search finds it as the only fast track. A per-pixel time term finds WISE 0855 and Epsilon Indi B blind. Synthetic movers are recovered about 77% of the time at peak signal-to-noise 10.

Features: play, blink, difference and stack views; Before/After comparison; spectra and light curves on click; live lookup for new patches; eight automatic candidate checks and a status ladder (Flagged, Passed automatic checks, Confirmed by community, Reviewed by team, Known, Artifact, Unexplained); anonymous advisory voting; nothing is sent to any agency automatically, and experts are pointed to Backyard Worlds and the Minor Planet Center. A brown dwarf score is included as an analysis, tested on two brown dwarfs.

Limits: our blind search misses Barnard's Star (saturated), engine speeds are low and used for detection only, synthetic tests are idealised, the false-alarm rate is an upper bound, and the demo asteroid was chosen by hand because the archive search was down at the time.
